title: How to Find Your Purpose & Design the Life You Want
guest: Suzy Welch, NYU Stern professor, former editor in chief of Harvard Business Review, author of Becoming You and creator of the Values Bridge
summary: Suzy Welch walks the sisters through their Values Bridge results (16 rank-ordered values like radius, achievement, eudaimonia, affluence, beholderism, belovedness, scope) and explains how the Becoming You method combines values, aptitudes and economically viable interests to find purpose. The conversation then covers why people settle into B-plus lives until a crisis, the Four Horsemen of dream destruction, her money rules (no last best deal, cut your losses), how she and Jack Welch worked as partners, and her own reinventions including being fired from HBR and dating after widowhood.

ideas.idea: Purpose comes from synthesizing three data sets: your values, your aptitudes and your economically viable interests.
ideas.detail: This is the core of the Becoming You class at NYU Stern, which had an 800-student waitlist and is now taught in mega sections; the Values Bridge tool rank-orders 16 values and shows how much you are living each one.

ideas.idea: The 'authenticity gap' is the distance between how much you hold a value and how much you are actually living it, and it is the source of the 'off' feeling in many lives.
ideas.detail: Welch describes students with voice or belovedness as their number one value but a 98-99% authenticity gap, meaning they want it and cannot live it.

ideas.idea: Partners should have matching levels of strongly presenting values like radius, beholderism and belovedness, or the relationship will be a constant fight over what matters.
ideas.detail: The Values Bridge gives couples a conflict or harmony score; her daughter and fiance share their top six values, while Cherie's early-20s boyfriend mocked her big dreams and would have scored near 100% conflict. Welch's advice: give a serious partner the test.

ideas.idea: Achievement (wanting visible success) is a value that business schools select for, even though Gen Z ranks it around number 11 of 16.
ideas.detail: Both sisters rank achievement in their top four, hence the name Tiger Sisters; Welch has it at number two herself and notes her Gen Z students ask 'who needs that?'

ideas.idea: Eudaimonia (self-care, recreation, pleasure, sex) typically conflicts with affluence and achievement, and people who rank all of them high must consciously work out the trade-off.
ideas.detail: Welch has eudaimonia at 15 because her joy is in her work; Jean notes her banking background trained her to set self-care aside for achievement, while Cherie's Gen Z-adjacent cohort prizes work-life balance.

ideas.idea: Beholderism, caring deeply about how things look including yourself, is often a proxy for wanting harmony and control in a chaotic world, and it is the top value of almost every influencer.
ideas.detail: Jean's top value is beholderism; she read interior design books at 12 and moves flowers that clash with a room. Welch says no value is good or bad, and that naming it lets you explain yourself to others.

ideas.idea: A values mismatch with your employer means going to work every day 'in a suit three sizes too small', so use your values to test whether you will last at an organization.
ideas.detail: People with high achievement and affluence and low voice fit investment banks like Goldman Sachs; someone with very high voice will find that a different kind of fit.

ideas.idea: Values are mostly stable from about age 25, but a seismic life event such as a death, divorce, child or broken engagement can reshuffle them temporarily.
ideas.detail: Welch's belovedness fell to 16 after her husband died; Jean's is at 11 a year after ending an eight-year engagement, which Welch expects to move back up within six to twelve months.

ideas.idea: Knowing your values is not enough; you also have to know your aptitudes, both cognitive and personality strengths, because you can be bad at a job purely because of your personality.
ideas.detail: Her example: you could want to be Celine Dion and have a very bad voice.

ideas.idea: The Four Horsemen of dream destruction that stop you living your own life are expectations, expedience, events and economic security.
ideas.detail: Expectations from family, taking the easy job that recruits you, events like layoffs or babies that push you off course, and money decisions even when money does not matter to you. She offers a free quiz to identify which horseman is at work.

ideas.idea: People habitually live B-plus lives for decades and usually need a crisis such as a firing, divorce or breakup to start the self-examination; do the work before the crisis.
ideas.detail: Jean says her life looked A-plus from outside (beautiful couple, high-powered job, LA) and it took her engagement ending to see it was not her true self; Welch says otherwise she would have been 45 crying in her car asking 'what have I done?'

ideas.idea: When you are living your own life you feel 'exquisitely alive', and that internal signal, not friends and parents checking boxes, is the real test.
ideas.detail: The outside world confirms your life is perfect while you know inside; if you have never felt that aliveness you do not even know what you are missing.

ideas.idea: There is no universal work-life balance; the question is what is your balance, and you should give yourself permission to live it without judging others.
ideas.detail: She cites Jensen Huang saying 'I love my work life balance, I work all the time' and says the rank-ordered values let people admit they want fame, money and achievement over eudaimonia. Affluence and eudaimonia rarely track together without inherited wealth.

ideas.idea: Social media makes you compare yourself against lives built on values you do not actually hold; check the envy against your own rank order.
ideas.detail: Cherie feels a pang seeing 20-person bachelorette parties but belonging is her lowest value; Welch's high-radius daughter is having a wedding with no bridesmaids and no parties because that is not who they are.

ideas.idea: Money rule one: there is no last best deal, so refuse the frenzy that advertisers, realtors and stock sellers create.
ideas.detail: She says this frame has saved her from many wrong turns, especially in real estate, because there will always be another house and another good deal.

ideas.idea: Money rule two: fight the sunk cost fallacy and cut your losses the moment you know you made a mistake, publicly owning it.
ideas.detail: She sold a house after two years and real renovation spending, telling friends 'I made a mistake, I'm out, I may take a hit.' Decision science shows we are wired to pour more money on problems; resisting is a discipline that applies to jobs and relationships too.

ideas.idea: 'No last best deal' applies to love: believing this partner is the last one available makes you settle, and settling never leads anywhere good.
ideas.detail: A 55-year-old friend stayed with a man who treated her terribly because 'who else is there going to be'; he left her for a younger woman and she later happily found someone else.

ideas.idea: A dual-career couple works by sharing values, talking constantly, knowing their lanes and deeply respecting each other's expertise.
ideas.detail: She was never CEO of GE managing 400,000 people and Jack had never written or edited books; they let each other be good at what they were good at. It also helped that Jack had high agency while she is low-agency and consensus-driven.

ideas.idea: In disagreements, start from the inside mantra 'maybe he's right' and hear the other person out without defensiveness; it often makes them more open to your counterpoints.
ideas.detail: When Jack announced a changed vacation plan her gut said 'worst idea ever' but she asked why, listened, then laid out where they differed, and he often said 'I never thought of that.' It rests on trusting that he loved her and would never hurt her.

ideas.idea: Assuming good intent in strangers can change the trajectory of your life and career, even though you will occasionally get burned.
ideas.detail: Jack treated every stranger as a friend not yet met and found a party of strangers 'could anything be more exciting'; going in with your dukes up costs you relationships and conversations.

ideas.idea: Reinvention is mandatory because the economy, the world and you all change, and getting fired is a career death you can be reborn from as long as you tell the truth about it.
ideas.detail: Fired from Harvard Business Review in her 40s and reported in the Wall Street Journal, she refused a press release saying she resigned; two weeks later Oprah's organization called. She later earned a PhD in her 60s and says you can 'die 1000 times in your career.'

ideas.idea: After the worst thing has happened to you, fearlessness increases, so doing brave things like a first date after six years of widowhood is 'part of the Wisdom Project'.
ideas.detail: She nearly cancelled the date, referenced Jack 33 times, and the man astutely asked whether she was ready to be loved by anyone besides Jack; she is not averse to trying again. Wisdom, she says, comes from what she did wrong, not right.

ideas.idea: Building a business around helping people is addictive because the daily messages saying 'it changed my life' put you in a flow state.
ideas.detail: Since the Values Bridge launched on May 6 about 65,000-66,000 people have taken it and more products are coming; when her kids tell her to take a day off she says 'I'm building something.'

ideas.idea: Having a shared vocabulary for values lets people name what they know in their heart and build a bridge to understanding each other.
ideas.detail: A Stanford student connected the work to Wittgenstein's 'the limits of my language are the limits of my world'; the sisters say having the word eudaimonia lets them finally express something they felt.
